summary: Lists requirements for trait-based authorization in SIP, which decides what a participant may do based on their attributes. This allows richer policy decisions and more privacy for users than plain identity. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A club checks if you are over a certain age instead of asking for your whole name, so it learns only what it needs.

subtitle: Using attributes instead of identity to authorize access in SIP communications.

tldr.problem: Traditional SIP authorization asks "Who are you?" and checks a list of allowed users. In large federations of independent organizations, the receiving system doesn't know individual users and can't make access decisions. There is a need for authorization based on attributes (traits) like "faculty member" or "account in good standing" rather than fixed identity.
tldr.mechanism: An authorization service issues cryptographically signed assertions that claim certain attributes about a user (e.g., "this person is a faculty member"). These assertions travel with the SIP request. A receiving system checks the signature and makes authorization decisions based on the claimed attributes, not the user's identity.
tldr.outcome: This framework enables privacy-preserving authorization in federated systems. Users can prove they have needed attributes without revealing their identity. Organizations can make policy decisions based on roles and groups rather than maintaining lists of individual users.

today: RFC 4484 is an Informational RFC describing requirements that have influenced subsequent authorization and identity work in SIP. The framework remains relevant for federated environments requiring attribute-based access control.

sections.title: The Problem with Identity-Only Authorization
sections.content:
Traditional SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) authorization works like this: a caller sends a SIP request with an identity (such as their phone number or username). The receiving system looks up that identity in a database to see if the caller is allowed to make the request.

This works well within a single organization—a company knows all its employees. But on the Internet, most interactions are between organizations that don't know each other's users. A university and a hospital may want to share a video call service, but the hospital doesn't have a list of the university's 50,000 students. The university doesn't want to give the hospital detailed information about all its students. Yet the hospital wants to enforce a policy like "we will video-call with university faculty but not undergraduates."

Trait-based authorization solves this by letting the university assert attributes about the caller—"this person is a faculty member"—rather than divulging their identity. The hospital can then decide based on that trait alone.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way: You say your name, the club looks you up in their list. The new way: You show a card from your school saying "I am a teacher", and the club lets you in without knowing who you are.

sections.title: How Trait Assertions Work
sections.content:
The system has three key roles: an authorization service (issued by a trusted organization), a user agent client (UAC) (the person making the call), and a user agent server (UAS) (the recipient).

The process unfolds as follows: (1) The UAC authenticates to the authorization service (using standard SIP authentication or some other method). (2) The authorization service verifies the user's identity and attributes, then creates an assertion—a document asserting "this user has the traits: faculty, chemistry-department". (3) The authorization service digitally signs the assertion using its private key. (4) The UAC includes this signed assertion in the SIP request. (5) The UAS receives the request, verifies the authorization service's signature, and checks whether it trusts that service. (6) If the UAS trusts the issuer, it examines the traits in the assertion and makes an authorization decision based on its policies.

Multiple organizations that trust each other form a federation—they agree to recognize each other's assertions. This eliminates the need to maintain shared lists of individual users while enabling rich policy decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: 1. You log into the school system. 2. The school says "Okay, you're a teacher" and gives you a signed paper saying so. 3. You take that paper to the hospital video service. 4. The hospital checks the school's signature, sees "teacher", and lets you book a call because their policy allows teachers.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Settlement for services: When one telecom operator routes calls to another's conference bridge, they may need real-time settlement. The calling domain can assert that a user has "an account in good standing" rather than sending account numbers, enabling the called domain to settle billing without handling sensitive financial data.

Gateway authentication: A telephone company operates PSTN-to-SIP gateways. Each gateway should be authorized based on the trait "is a gateway", rather than requiring individual certificates for thousands of gateways or relying on hostname conventions.

Resource-constrained access: Two universities share a video-conference service over limited bandwidth. They want to enforce a policy like "faculty can start conferences, staff can join, students can only attend". Rather than maintaining a shared list of all students and staff, each university can assert the role of the requester.

Priority and precedence: A network operator might assign higher priority to certain calls. An assertion trait "priority-1" can travel with the request and be used to make QoS decisions, without disclosing the user's identity.

Single sign-on: A user authenticates to the SIP service via an authorization assertion. The same assertion can be reused in related protocols—for example, to request QoS from the network—without re-authenticating.
sections.plainLanguage: Examples: A hospital saying "this doctor is legit so you can route their call to us." A university saying "this person teaches here." A bank saying "this customer's account is good." All without telling the other organization who the specific person is.

sections.title: Requirements for SIP Trait Authorization
sections.content:
RFC 4484 specifies 18 requirements. Key ones include:

Assertion mechanics: SIP UACs and authorization services MUST be able to embed and deliver assertions in SIP requests (by value or by reference). Authorization services MUST authenticate clients before issuing assertions. Intermediaries (proxy servers) MUST be able to inspect and evaluate assertions when authorized to do so.

Assertion schemes: There MUST be a single baseline mandatory-to-implement assertion format (the RFC suggests SAML or X.509 Attribute Certificates). Other assertion schemes MAY be supported.

Trait control: Assertions MUST be capable of asserting attributes and traits associated with a user's identity. Users MUST be able to specify policies to authorization services about which traits to share with which destinations. Different recipients MAY see different subsets of traits from the same user.

Privacy and security: It MUST be possible to present an assertion with no identity information—only traits. The mechanism MUST prevent unauthorized parties from viewing assertion contents. All assertions MUST be cryptographically signed by the issuing authorization service, providing non-repudiation and integrity.

Reference integrity: There MUST be a way to verify that an assertion belongs to the SIP request it accompanies (e.g., that it authorizes this specific message and not some other one). Multiple assertions from different authorization services MAY be attached to a single request.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must: let you carry a signed statement in your SIP message, let authorization servers verify you before signing, let you control who sees which traits, and prevent anyone from faking or modifying the statement.

sections.title: Security Model
sections.content:
The security of trait-based authorization depends on several factors:

Trust in authorization services: A UAS trusts an assertion only if it trusts the authorization service that signed it. This trust relationship is typically established through membership in a federation with agreed-upon policies.

Signature verification: Every assertion MUST be digitally signed by the authorizing service. Recipients verify the signature using the service's public key before accepting the assertion.

Reference integrity: An assertion must be cryptographically bound to the SIP request it authorizes, preventing an attacker from attaching one user's assertion to another user's request.

Selective disclosure: An authorization service can issue different versions of an assertion to different recipients. For example, it might provide only the trait "student" to a videoconferencing provider, withholding the student's major, GPA, and identity.

End-to-end protection: If assertions are carried in SIP request bodies, they are protected end-to-end and cannot be viewed by intermediaries. If assertions are referenced (e.g., via HTTP URL), access control can be applied to the URL itself, allowing the service provider to control who can access which assertion details.
sections.plainLanguage: Trust is everything: you only believe the signed statement if you trust the organization that signed it. The signature prevents forgery. Only the right people see sensitive traits. And the statement travels with your message so someone can't swap it for another statement.
